chapter: Picnics, wagon advertising and saloon work
title: The Tipperary night: playing the pianola and a parlor job offer
summary: During the Shriners' visit he plays the saloon piano instead of violin, packs the house, and is offered a job playing parlor piano.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Yes, I played, I'll tell you, the scene on the job, I played at Arborville. Oh yes, you were. Well it happened once the Shriners came to town. I had two bartenders at McIshies. I had a day bartender and a night bartender. Well, the night bartender, him and his lady friend, they were live parties. They'd go out shopping and they'd stop in the 10 cent store. During that time the Shriners was here and the pop, the piece of the Shriners was a long way to Tipperary and people was buying them songs, man, like hotcakes. So, it was the bartender, Johnny Rice was his name. And his lady friend. Well they bought a copy. Well in that saloon, they had a pianola. But it was always kept locked. Well, on a Monday night, Johnny Rice and his lady friend, they went out shopping, bought a song, they came down that night. And he asked the bass player, say, Ike. We is out today, say, here's the pop, the song, the Shriners, a long way to Tipperary. Well, the man of the player they had, he was an air player. They'd play their own stuff with their hair and things. So, on that time I was there, Ike told him, say, well listen, our violin player will play that for you. If you open that piano. So, he got the key and you open that piano. And, uh, just a little, just like you come off the street in here. And I started playing it. And the Shriners started piling in there, plus all the shipments, you know. And it got packed. And they were throwing dollars around there that night, like shims. And I didn't have to touch my violin at all. I put it in the case and just proceed all that night on the piano. So, he drove, Mr. Lula's old man. He started to crowd raise, stand around. So, he got in the midst, they called me outside. We used to wear, had a locker, go there, and you got a dress coat on, put a little white coat on. So. What kind of white coat?
What did you wear exactly? What did you wear? Huh? What did you wear exactly?
We'd have a white jacket on.
Like a dinner jacket? Or a waiter's jacket? Or a...
Or a little white coat. Or a little white coat. Like a summer coat.
What kind of trousers? Well, I wore trousers, but we... Well, whatever you had.
What we had on. I see.
Only we just changed our dress coat, you see.
Did you wear a tie? Oh, yeah. Big tie?
Yeah. We wear, we wear a tie. We just took our coat on, you know. A little white coat on. So he says, well listen. He liked it in my playing.

So he said, how would you like to play a job, play in the parlor? He said, you wouldn't wear no white coat, you could stay dressed. Well, no one's at the house, at your leisure, you can go back in the set room and read magazines. You can step out to the corner, it'll give you a buzz when comfort comes.
